bib.title: A Neural Network Solves, Explains, and Generates University Math Problems by Program Synthesis and Few-Shot Learning at Human Level

read.skipped: Main text (about 39k chars) read closely; appendix tables 3 onward (per-question Codex input, code, explanation, GPT-3 response; generated questions) skimmed, as they are per-item listings.

question: Can a language model pre-trained on text and fine-tuned on code solve, explain and generate university-level math course questions by synthesizing programs?
hypothesis: Text-only pre-training is why earlier transformers failed at advanced math; a code-tuned model that writes programs will solve them.
contributions: Codex with program synthesis and few-shot learning automatically solves 81% of randomly sampled questions from six MIT courses and one Columbia course
Same method reaches 81.1% on sampled MATH topics versus a prior 8.8%
Pipeline to explain solution programs and generate new questions, evaluated by a student survey
New dataset of course questions, including an unreleased Columbia course

method.summary: Each question is given to Codex as-is or with an automatic prefix (write a program, using sympy, using simulations) inside a Python docstring; the generated program is run and its output compared with the answer. If zero-shot fails, up to five solved question-code pairs from the same course, chosen by embedding cosine similarity, are added as few-shot examples. Unsolved questions (19%) are manually tidied. Explanations and new questions are also generated by Codex.
method.task: university math course problem solving by program synthesis; explanation; question generation

datasets.name: MIT and Columbia course questions
datasets.split: random sample, excluding questions with images or requiring proofs
datasets.preprocessing: Zero-shot input as-is or with automatic prefixes; 19% manually tidied or interactively prompted

models.name: OpenAI Codex code-davinci-002
models.architecture: transformer pre-trained on text, fine-tuned on code

inference.decoding: solution and explanation: top P 0 and temperature 0 (deterministic); frequency and presence penalties 0; no stop sequences
inference.temperature: 0 for solving and explaining; 0.1 for question generation
inference.top_p: 0 for solving and explaining; 0.1 for question generation
inference.samples: one deterministic generation per question; for few-shot, examples are added one at a time until the output is correct, up to five
inference.prompting: Prompt is a Python docstring in triple quotes. Zero-shot: question as-is, or prefixed with 'write a program', 'using sympy', or 'using simulations'. Few-shot: question-code examples, then target question. GPT-3 CoT: 'Let's think step by step.' appended after few-shot questions and answers and the new question.
inference.retrieval: cosine similarity of text-similarity-babbage-001 embeddings of questions; nearest solved question from the same course first, then next nearest, up to 5

other.explanation_prompt: question, generated code, then triple quotes and 'Here is what the above code is doing: 1.'
other.generation_prompt: 25 randomly selected solved problems as a numbered list, cut after a random question, Codex completes the next

metrics.name: automatic solve rate
metrics.definition: fraction of questions for which the printed output or returned value of the generated program is the correct answer, without manual prompt edits

metrics.name: survey rating
metrics.definition: 15 students rate 60 questions (5 human and 5 generated per MIT course): human vs machine, appropriate or not, difficulty 1 to 5

baselines: previous MATH state of the art 8.8% (Hendrycks et al. 2021)
eval.protocol: Totals shown with standard errors; correctness judged by running the program; no repeated runs reported; survey with 95% confidence intervals.

prompts.text: Here is what the above code is doing: 1.
prompts.where: Methods, Automatic Explanation (paraphrased as three quotes followed by the text 'Here is what the above code is doing: 1.')

results.claim: Codex few-shot program synthesis automatically solves 81% of course questions.
results.setup: 175 course questions: 25 randomly sampled from each of 18.01, 18.02, 18.03, 18.05, 18.06, 6.042, COMS3251; Codex code-davinci-002, temperature 0, program executed in Python; zero-shot first then few-shot with up to 5 examples
results.quote: achieve automatic solve rates on the MIT math courses (A) 71.1% with zero-shot learning and 81.1% with few-shot learning
results.note: Abstract and text say 81%. Remaining 19% are manually prompted, so 81% is not a single-shot rate.

results.claim: Zero-shot Codex solves 71.1% of course questions.
results.setup: 175 course questions: 25 randomly sampled from each of 18.01, 18.02, 18.03, 18.05, 18.06, 6.042, COMS3251; Codex code-davinci-002, temperature 0, program executed in Python

results.claim: GPT-3 text-davinci-002 zero-shot solves 18.8% of the course questions.
results.setup: same 175 course questions, GPT-3 text-davinci-002 answering in text

results.claim: Fifteen students completed the survey rating 60 questions.
results.setup: student survey of human-written vs Codex-generated questions, 5 of each per MIT course
results.note: Effect sizes are only in Fig. 7; the text reports them qualitatively.

limits: Cannot solve image questions, questions needing proofs, or computationally intractable problems.
Only 25 questions per course and 15 per MATH topic; sample sizes are small and the 81% includes 19% manually tidied or interactively prompted.
Few-shot examples are added until output matches the known answer, so the few-shot rate uses answer feedback.
Zero-shot allows trying several prefixes; selection among prompts is not separated from the rate.
Temperature 0 so one run per question; no variance over runs is reported.
Codex may have seen public course material; only COMS3251 is argued to be unseen, and it is the only separate check.
Survey is 15 participants; human-level claim rests on it and on comparison to typical student performance, which is asserted not measured.
MATH baseline 8.8% is not on the same sample.
